title: Competitive Safety Analysis: Robust Decision-Making in Multi-Agent Systems
review_status: full-text audit complete; JAIR publication chronology, safety-level/Nash conditions, competitive-ratio definitions, load-balancing theorem and scope limitations checked
sections_checked: Title page and publication metadata: JAIR 17 (2002), pp. 363–378; arXiv first submitted 2011-06-22
Abstract and Sections 2–6: safety levels and stated 2×2/set-theoretic game conditions
Section 7: competitive-safety definition and extended decentralized load-balancing theorem
Section 8 and conclusion: Bayesian-game example and scope
venue_year_verified: Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, volume 17 (2002), pages 363–378; arXiv first submitted 2011-06-22
evidence_note: For generic non-reducible 2×2 games the safety-level value equals a Nash-equilibrium payoff when the safety-level strategy is strictly mixed; the paper explicitly says this need not hold for pure safety-level strategies. It proves a 9/8-competitive safety strategy for its extended decentralized load-balancing setting. These are model-specific mathematical results, not deployment measurements.

title: Interactive POMDP Lite: Towards Practical Planning to Predict and Exploit Intentions for Interacting with Self-Interested Agents
review_status: full-text audit complete; IJCAI venue, nested-MDP/I-POMDP Lite assumptions, policy-loss bound, intersection and stochastic-game experiments, and scope limitations checked
sections_checked: Title/abstract and IJCAI 2013 proceedings metadata, pp. 2298–2305
Sections 2–3: nested MDP and I-POMDP Lite modeling assumptions and complexity
Section 4: Theorem 4 policy-loss bound and definition of prediction error
Sections 5–6: 800-episode scripted intersection evaluation, POSG experiments and conclusion
evidence_note: Theorem 4 bounds I-POMDP Lite policy loss linearly in opponent-strategy prediction error, with other model/problem factors. Evaluation includes 800 episodes in a 7×7 intersection with a scripted human-driver model and a series of POSGs; no human participants are reported. The result is conditional on model assumptions and prediction quality.

title: Drake: An Efficient Executive for Temporal Plans with Choice
review_status: full-text audit complete; JAIR chronology, labeled temporal-network representation, benchmark sizes/hardware, compiled-size reductions and compilation/dispatch outliers checked
sections_checked: Title page and publication metadata: JAIR 42 (2011), pp. 607–659; arXiv first submitted 2014-01-18
Sections 2–7: labeled temporal-network compiler and dispatcher
Section 8.2: generated benchmark sizes, implementation/hardware, memory, compilation and dispatch results
venue_year_verified: Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, volume 42 (2011), pages 607–659; arXiv first submitted 2014-01-18
evidence_note: On random structured benchmarks the compiled representation is up to about 700× smaller in the largest cases, with many cases around 1–10 kB. Results are variable: a few compile cases take hours, some are up to 100× slower, and a few dispatch-latency outliers reach tens of seconds. The authors caution that application performance depends on plan structure.
